reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A degeneration in which calcium (hydroxyapatite) is deposited at the level of the Bowman layer in the interpalpebral band across the cornea
The band begins peripherally with a clear lucid interval separating it from the limbus and spreads centrally over time
Characteristic small clear holes (Swiss-cheese appearance) within the plaque correspond to nerves penetrating the Bowman layer
Common ocular causes include chronic anterior uveitis (especially juvenile idiopathic arthritis-associated), long-standing keratitis, and phthisical or chronically inflamed eyes
Systemic causes relate to raised calcium or phosphate, including hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D excess) and chronic renal failure
Symptoms include foreign body sensation, irritation, and reduced vision when the band crosses the visual axis; the surface may break down
Management is chelation with topical EDTA to remove superficial calcium, with phototherapeutic keratectomy for deeper or recurrent deposits, alongside treatment of the underlying cause
Recurrence is common if the underlying ocular inflammation or systemic calcium disturbance is not controlled
reference.pathophysiology: Band keratopathy results from the deposition of calcium salts, chiefly hydroxyapatite, in and beneath the Bowman layer within the interpalpebral zone of the cornea. Evaporation of tears in the exposed interpalpebral strip raises local pH and concentrates calcium and phosphate, favouring precipitation, while chronic ocular inflammation and elevated serum calcium or phosphate promote deposition. Calcification typically begins at the periphery with a clear zone next to the limbus and advances centrally as a horizontal band, sparing regions where nerves pierce the Bowman layer, which appear as clear holes. As the band thickens it disrupts the epithelium and reduces vision when it reaches the visual axis.
additionalDifferentials: Calcific plaques from chronic exposure or scarring
Anterior corneal dystrophies affecting the Bowman layer
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting the interpalpebral calcific band with lucid interval and clear holes
Serum calcium, phosphate, and albumin to detect hypercalcaemia or altered calcium-phosphate product
Parathyroid hormone and vitamin D assessment when a metabolic cause is suspected
Renal function tests to identify chronic renal failure
Evaluation for underlying uveitis or chronic ocular inflammation
Investigation for sarcoidosis or other systemic causes of hypercalcaemia when indicated
redFlags: Band encroaching on the visual axis with progressive visual loss
Surface breakdown with pain and risk of secondary infection
Underlying hypercalcaemia signalling a serious systemic disorder requiring investigation
Rapid recurrence indicating uncontrolled ocular inflammation or metabolic disturbance
reference.prognosis: Removal of superficial calcium by chelation or phototherapeutic keratectomy usually improves comfort and vision, but band keratopathy tends to recur unless the underlying ocular inflammation or systemic calcium disturbance is controlled.
pitfalls: Treating the cornea without investigating and addressing an underlying cause such as hypercalcaemia or chronic uveitis
Overlooking juvenile idiopathic arthritis-associated uveitis in a child with band keratopathy
Attempting deep removal that risks scarring when superficial chelation would suffice
Failing to anticipate recurrence when the driving condition persists
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Remove symptomatic superficial calcium by chelation with topical EDTA after epithelial debridement
Use phototherapeutic keratectomy for dense, recurrent or visually significant calcification
Treat the underlying ocular inflammation, controlling chronic anterior uveitis to reduce recurrence
Correct the underlying systemic calcium or phosphate disturbance such as hyperparathyroidism, sarcoidosis, vitamin D excess or chronic renal failure
Provide ocular surface lubrication and a bandage contact lens or analgesia for surface breakdown and foreign-body sensation
Monitor for recurrence and continue management of the causative condition
